title: Governance and Compliance (Basic): Azure Policy, Locks, Tags and Microsoft Purview
reading:
Today's menu

By the end of this lunch you will be able to:

- Explain what cloud governance means and decide which tool answers which question: Azure RBAC, Azure Policy or a resource lock.
- Describe the building blocks of Azure Policy — definitions, initiatives, assignments, scopes, parameters, compliance and exemptions.
- Choose a policy effect (Deny, Audit, Modify, Append, DeployIfNotExists, AuditIfNotExists, Disabled) for a requirement and predict when it runs.
- Design a small tagging strategy and enforce it with policy instead of good intentions.
- Describe what Microsoft Purview, the Service Trust Portal and the Microsoft Privacy Statement are for, and what replaces Azure Blueprints.

Meanwhile at Nusantara Retail

Monday morning, and Ibu Sari forwards you two e-mails. The first is from finance: last month's Azure invoice has a storage line in West Europe that nobody can explain, and half of the resources carry no tags, so nobody knows which department should pay for them. The second is from Nusantara Retail's legal advisor, reminding everyone that customer data must stay in approved regions close to home.

You dig in. Dewi created a test storage account in West Europe because it was near the top of a drop-down list, then forgot about it. Rizky, the contractor, almost deleted the resource group that holds the orders database while "tidying up" — he had the permissions, so nothing stopped him. Nobody did anything malicious. There were simply no guardrails.

Ibu Sari's question is short: "Can Azure stop these mistakes before they happen — and prove to an auditor that it did?" Today you answer it with Azure Policy, tags, locks and a first look at Microsoft Purview.

Reading

1. Governance means guardrails, not gates

Before the cloud, governance at Nusantara Retail was a locked server room and Pak Budi's signature on every purchase order. Nothing reached production without crossing his desk. In Azure, anyone with the right role can create a database in thirty seconds, from a laptop, at midnight. That speed is why you moved to the cloud, so you do not want the signature back. You want guardrails: rules the platform enforces automatically, so the safe path is also the easy path.

Cloud governance is the set of rules, processes and tools that keeps your use of Azure aligned with the business: costs stay predictable, data stays where the law wants it, and security settings do not drift. Compliance is the part where you can prove it — to an auditor, a regulator or your own director — with evidence instead of promises.

Each governance question maps to a specific tool:

Question | Tool | What it looks at | Example at Nusantara Retail
Who may do this? | Azure role-based access control (RBAC) — Lunch 05 | the identity making the request and its role at that scope | Rizky gets Contributor on the test resource group only
Is the result allowed to exist? | Azure Policy | the properties of the resource being created or changed, no matter who asks | storage accounts only in Southeast Asia or Indonesia Central
Must this never be deleted or changed by accident? | Resource lock | delete (or any write) operations on a locked scope, for everyone | nobody can delete the orders database, not even an Owner
What is it, and who pays for it? | Tags | name/value labels on resources | costCenter=CC-1001 on everything the storefront uses
Where is our sensitive data, and who touches it? | Microsoft Purview | the data itself, across Azure, Microsoft 365 and beyond | find every file that contains customer phone numbers

The first three work together on every request. When Dewi runs az storage account create, Azure Resource Manager (Lunch 04) authenticates her with Microsoft Entra ID, checks her RBAC permissions, and then evaluates policy assignments and locks before anything reaches the storage resource provider. A role says Dewi may create storage accounts; a policy can still say this storage account, in West Europe, may not exist. Every check must say yes.

Tip: When a deployment fails, the error code tells you which guardrail stopped it: AuthorizationFailed points to RBAC, RequestDisallowedByPolicy to Azure Policy (the message names the assignment that blocked you), and ScopeLocked to a lock. Read the code before you ask anyone for more permissions.

2. Azure Policy: definitions, initiatives and assignments

Azure Policy has three objects you will meet everywhere.

A policy definition is a rule written in JSON. It has an if part — a condition on resource properties, such as "the location is not in this list" — and a then part, the effect that happens when the condition is true. Azure ships thousands of built-in definitions that Microsoft maintains, such as Allowed locations and Require a tag on resources. When nothing fits, you write a custom definition. Parameters make a definition reusable: Allowed locations does not hard-code a region; it asks for a list when you use it.

An initiative (the CLI and the API call it a policy set) groups definitions that serve one goal, so you manage them as a single item. Microsoft publishes regulatory initiatives that map the controls of a standard to policies — for example ISO/IEC 27001, PCI DSS, and the Microsoft cloud security benchmark that Defender for Cloud (Lunch 15) assigns by default. A retailer that takes card payments, like Nusantara Retail, pays close attention to the PCI DSS one.

An assignment is where a definition or initiative starts working. It connects the rule to a scope — a management group, subscription, resource group or single resource — and supplies the parameter values: "Allowed locations, on the production subscription, with Indonesia Central and Southeast Asia." Everything below the scope inherits the assignment, just as role assignments inherit (Lunch 04). An assignment can also carry exclusions (child scopes it skips), a custom non-compliance message that appears in the error, and an enforcement mode: Default enforces the effect, while DoNotEnforce only reports, which is how you test a new rule without breaking anyone's deployment.

Three details trip up almost everyone. First, the mode of a definition decides what it evaluates. Tag and location rules usually use Indexed mode, which only looks at resource types that support tags and locations — and skips resource groups. That is why Allowed locations does not stop anyone creating a resource group in West Europe; a separate built-in, Allowed locations for resource groups, does that. Second, a resource group's location is only where its metadata lives. The resources inside can sit in any region, so restricting the group alone protects nothing. Third, assignments stack. When several assignments apply to a resource, each one is evaluated on its own and the result is the most restrictive combination. A team cannot "opt out" of a subscription-level Deny by assigning a friendlier policy to its own resource group; only an exclusion or an exemption on the original assignment can do that.

To find a built-in, open Policy › Definitions in the portal and filter by category (Tags, General, Storage…), or search from Cloud Shell with az policy definition list. Read the description and the parameters before you assign anything — the display name rarely tells the whole story.

3. Effects: what happens when a rule matches

The effect is the rule's answer. Choosing the right one is most of the skill.

Effect | What it does | When it acts | Use it when…
Deny | Blocks the create or update request; existing resources are only reported | before the request reaches the resource provider | the rule is non-negotiable, such as data residency
Audit | Lets the request through and marks the resource non-compliant | after Deny, before the resource provider | you want visibility first, or the rule is advice
Modify | Adds, replaces or removes tags and some properties in the request; fixes existing resources through remediation | before Deny | the fix can be automatic, such as copying a tag
Append | Adds fields to the request, but cannot fix existing resources | before Deny | a built-in still uses it; for tags, prefer Modify
AuditIfNotExists | After deployment, checks that a related resource exists and reports if it is missing | after the resource provider succeeds | VMs should have the Azure Monitor Agent, but you only want to know
DeployIfNotExists | After deployment, deploys the missing related resource with a template; fixes existing resources through remediation | after the resource provider succeeds | every database should send its logs to the central workspace
Disabled | Switches the rule off without deleting the assignment | checked first | you need to pause a rule whose effect is a parameter

The order matters. Azure Policy checks Disabled first, then lets Append and Modify change the request, then evaluates Deny, then Audit. AuditIfNotExists and DeployIfNotExists run only after the resource provider reports success. Because Modify runs before Deny, a Modify rule that adds a missing tag can turn a request that a Deny rule would have blocked into one that passes. You will see exactly this in the lab.

A few newer effects exist for special cases: DenyAction blocks delete requests on matching resources, Manual lets you attest to controls that cannot be checked automatically, and Mutate and addToNetworkGroup serve AKS and Azure Virtual Network Manager.

Modify and DeployIfNotExists change things on your behalf, so their assignment needs a managed identity (Lunch 15) holding the roles the definition lists. New and updated resources are handled as they arrive. Resources that existed before the assignment are only reported until you run a remediation task, which uses that identity to fix them in bulk.

Compliance is the report card. Each resource gets a compliance state per assignment — Compliant, Non-compliant, Exempt, Not started and a few rarer ones. Evaluation happens when a resource is created or updated (results appear about 15 minutes later), when an assignment is created or changed (it takes about five minutes to apply, then the scan begins), once every 24 hours for everything, and on demand with az policy state trigger-scan. When a resource legitimately cannot comply — a two-week marketing test that needs another region — you grant an exemption instead of weakening the rule. Waiver means "we accept this for now"; Mitigated means "we meet the intent another way"; an expiry date makes sure nobody forgets. Lunch 31 goes deeper.

4. Tags and locks: label everything, protect what matters

A tag is a name/value pair — costCenter=CC-1001 — that you attach to a subscription, resource group or resource (but not to a management group). Tags cost nothing and power a lot: cost reports grouped by department (Lunch 19), automation that stops environment=dev machines at night, and queries that answer "what belongs to the storefront?". Four rules to remember:

- Resources do not inherit their resource group's tags. If you want inheritance, a policy has to do it.
- Each resource, resource group or subscription holds up to 50 tags. Names are case-insensitive but values are case-sensitive, so Finance and finance end up as two different lines in a cost report.
- Tags are plain text that shows up in exports, logs and invoices. Never put a secret in a tag.
- Not every resource type supports tags. Check the documentation before you build a rule around one.

A tagging strategy is short on purpose. Nusantara Retail starts with four mandatory tags:

Tag | Example value | Why it exists
costCenter | CC-1001 (e-commerce) | finance charges the right department
environment | prod, test or dev | automation and alerts treat them differently
owner | team-storefront | someone answers when the resource misbehaves
dataClassification | confidential | anything holding customer data gets extra scrutiny

Policy turns the strategy into reality. Require a tag on resources (Deny) refuses untagged resources. Add a tag to resources and Inherit a tag from the resource group if missing (both Modify) fill the gap automatically, so people only have to tag the resource group. Combine an inherit rule with a require rule and you get convenience plus a backstop.

A resource lock protects what must not change by accident. CanNotDelete (Delete in the portal) allows reads and updates but blocks deletion; ReadOnly (Read-only) blocks every write. Locks apply to subscriptions, resource groups and resources, are inherited by everything below, and override RBAC — even an Owner must remove the lock first. Only roles with Microsoft.Authorization/locks/* permissions, such as Owner and User Access Administrator, can create or delete them.

Warning: Locks are blunter than they look. A ReadOnly lock blocks operations that use POST, so it stops you listing storage account keys, starting or restarting VMs in a locked resource group, or scaling an App Service plan. A CanNotDelete lock on one resource blocks deletion of its whole resource group. And locks protect only the control plane: someone with data access can still delete the blobs inside a "locked" storage account. Locks prevent accidents; backups (Lunch 17) recover from them.

5. Beyond resource settings: Microsoft Purview, the Service Trust Portal and the privacy statement

Azure Policy governs how resources are configured. It cannot tell you that a CSV file in a storage account holds 40,000 customer phone numbers, or that someone e-mailed it outside the company. That is the job of Microsoft Purview, Microsoft's family of data governance, data security and data compliance solutions. It works across Azure, Microsoft 365, on-premises sources and other clouds, and you manage it in the Microsoft Purview portal.

Area | Capability | What it does | Nusantara Retail example
Data governance | Data Map | scans data sources and classifies what it finds | discover which databases and storage accounts hold customer data
Data governance | Unified Catalog | a searchable catalog with owners, glossary terms and data quality | Dewi finds the trusted orders dataset instead of copying a stale one
Data security | Information Protection (sensitivity labels) | labels and protects documents and data by sensitivity | the loyalty-member export is labelled Confidential
Data security | Data Loss Prevention | detects and blocks risky sharing of sensitive information | card numbers cannot leave by e-mail
Data security | Insider Risk Management | spots risky user activity | someone who is leaving downloads the customer list
Data compliance | Compliance Manager | tracks your controls against regulations and scores progress | prepare for a personal-data-protection audit
Data compliance | Audit, eDiscovery, Data Lifecycle Management | records activity, finds content for legal cases, keeps or deletes data on schedule | keep invoices for the required period, then delete them

At AZ-900 level, remember the split: Azure Policy for resource configuration, Purview for the data itself.

Two Microsoft resources answer the question "how do we know Microsoft is compliant?". The Service Trust Portal (servicetrust.microsoft.com) publishes independent audit reports and certifications for Microsoft's cloud services — ISO/IEC 27001, SOC 1, 2 and 3, PCI DSS, CSA STAR and many regional ones — plus whitepapers. Some documents need a sign-in with a work account. When Nusantara Retail's auditor asks for proof that Azure's datacenters meet PCI DSS, that is where you send them. The Microsoft Privacy Statement (privacy.microsoft.com) explains what personal data Microsoft collects through its products, how it uses that data, and the choices people have. Together they cover Microsoft's half of the shared responsibility model; Azure Policy and Purview help you with yours.

Important: Azure Blueprints is retired — do not start anything new with it. Blueprints, a preview service that packaged policies, role assignments and templates, has blocked new definitions since July 31, 2026, blocks new assignments from October 31, 2026, and is fully retired on January 31, 2027. Use Azure Policy for the rules and deployment stacks, with template specs or Git for versioning, to deploy and protect resources as a unit. Lunch 20 shows stacks in action, and Lunch 31 covers migration.

6. How it fits together for Nusantara Retail

Back to Ibu Sari's question. Here is the first governance baseline you propose, and the tool that carries each rule:

Requirement | Tool and setting
Customer data stays close to home | Allowed locations (Deny) on the subscription: Indonesia Central for production, Southeast Asia for labs
Every cost is traceable | Inherit a tag from the resource group if missing (Modify) plus Require a tag on resources (Deny) for costCenter
The orders database survives a tidy-up | a CanNotDelete lock on its resource group
Contractors do only what they must | RBAC: Rizky gets Contributor on the test resource group only
Auditors get evidence | the Azure Policy compliance view, Defender for Cloud regulatory compliance, the Service Trust Portal
Sensitive data is known and protected | Microsoft Purview scans, planned for next quarter

Roll it out gently. Assign new rules in Audit or DoNotEnforce mode first, read the compliance report for a week, talk to the teams whose resources show up, and only then switch to Deny. Fix existing resources with remediation tasks rather than one-off scripts, so the fix is repeatable. When someone needs an exception, write an exemption with an expiry date instead of quietly removing the rule.

The baseline pays off in the next lunches: the costCenter tag drives the cost reports in Lunch 19, and in Lunch 20 you deploy rules and resources with Bicep and protect them with a deployment stack.

Pause and think: Dewi's pipeline creates a storage account without tags in rg-storefront-test, which is tagged costCenter=CC-1001. Both Require a tag on resources and Inherit a tag from the resource group if missing are assigned for costCenter. Does her deployment succeed? What changes if someone removes the tag from the resource group?

Ready for more? Lunch 31 · Governance at Scale takes these ideas to management groups, initiatives across many subscriptions, and policy as code.

Field notes from Stefanus

Every Deny needs a door. For each Deny rule in a governance design, I ask: who owns it, and what does a developer do at five on a Friday afternoon when it blocks something legitimate? If the answer is "open a ticket and wait", people find a way around the rule, usually with broader permissions or a test subscription nobody governs. So every Deny assignment gets a non-compliance message that says what to do instead, a named owner, and an exemption path with an expiry date. I keep tags just as lean: four that drive real decisions beat twenty that end up filled with "tbd". And my rule for locks is simple: CanNotDelete on whatever you cannot rebuild from code, such as databases and storage accounts that hold data, and ReadOnly almost never.

Go further

- Microsoft Learn: What is Azure Policy? (https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/governance/policy/overview) — the official overview, including how policy and RBAC differ and the limits per scope.
- Microsoft Learn: Azure Policy definitions effect basics (https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/governance/policy/concepts/effect-basics) — every effect, the order of evaluation and how layered assignments combine.
- Microsoft Learn: Lock your Azure resources to protect your infrastructure (https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/azure-resource-manager/management/lock-resources) — the full list of surprising things a lock blocks.
- Microsoft Learn: Learn about Microsoft Purview (https://learn.microsoft.com/purview/purview) — a tour of the data security, governance and compliance solutions.

quiz.q: Rizky has Contributor on the resource group that holds the orders database. You must make sure nobody — not even an Owner — deletes it by accident, while updates keep working. What do you use?
quiz.a: A CanNotDelete lock on the database (or on its resource group). Locks apply to everyone regardless of role, and CanNotDelete still allows reads and updates — removing Rizky's role would block his legitimate work too.

quiz.q: Finance wants every new resource to carry costCenter. Developers forget tags, but every resource group is tagged when it is created. Which built-in policies give the least friction, and what about resources that already exist?
quiz.a: Assign Inherit a tag from the resource group if missing (Modify), optionally backed by Require a tag on resources (Deny), and run a remediation task for the existing resources. Modify runs before Deny, so untagged requests in tagged groups are fixed instead of refused, and remediation handles what existed before the assignment.

quiz.q: You assign Allowed locations (Southeast Asia only) to the subscription. The next morning an existing storage account in West Europe shows as Non-compliant, but it still works. Why was it not removed, and what are your options?
quiz.a: Deny only blocks create and update requests; existing resources are evaluated and reported, never deleted. You either move or recreate the data in an allowed region and delete the old account, or grant a time-limited exemption (Waiver) if there is a business reason to keep it for now.

quiz.q: An auditor asks for an independent report showing that Microsoft's cloud services meet ISO/IEC 27001. Where do you send them?
quiz.a: To the Service Trust Portal. It publishes third-party audit reports and certifications for Microsoft's cloud services, whereas Microsoft Purview and Azure Policy are about your data and your resources.

quiz.q: A colleague proposes Azure Blueprints to stamp out a standard setup for the new loyalty-app subscription. What do you recommend?
quiz.a: Don't: Azure Blueprints is retired (no new assignments from October 31, 2026; fully retired January 31, 2027). Use Azure Policy for the rules and deployment stacks with template specs or Git for the resources, because that is Microsoft's recommended replacement.

takeaways: Azure RBAC decides who may act, Azure Policy decides what may exist, and resource locks protect what must not be deleted or changed by accident — use all three together.
A policy definition is an if/then rule, an initiative bundles definitions, and an assignment applies them to a scope with parameters; everything below the scope inherits the assignment.

The effect decides the response: Deny blocks, Audit reports, Modify and Append change the request first, and DeployIfNotExists and AuditIfNotExists check related resources after deployment. Modify and DeployIfNotExists need a managed identity, plus remediation tasks for resources that already exist.
Tags drive cost reports and automation but are not inherited — keep a short mandatory list and enforce it with policy.

Microsoft Purview governs and protects the data itself; the Service Trust Portal and the Microsoft Privacy Statement answer the auditor and the lawyer; Azure Blueprints is retired, so use policy plus deployment stacks.

lab.title: Keep data in the right place
lab.text:
What you'll build

Ibu Sari wants three guardrails before anyone deploys another resource: everything stays in the approved region, everything carries a costCenter tag for finance, and nobody has to remember to type that tag. You will put those rules on a lab resource group with three built-in Azure Policy definitions, prove that a deployment in the wrong region is refused, watch a Modify policy add a missing tag on its own, fix two "legacy" resources that existed before the rules with a remediation task, and read the compliance report an auditor would ask for.

Before you start

- An Azure subscription where you can create resources (see Lab 01 (https://stefpin.github.io/azure-fundamentals-lunches/en/labs/01-before-you-begin.html)) and where you are Owner (or Contributor plus User Access Administrator). The Modify assignment in Task 4 creates a role assignment for its managed identity, and plain Contributor cannot do that. Use a personal or dedicated lab subscription.
- Azure Cloud Shell (Bash) — open shell.azure.com. Nothing to install.
- Get the lab files and load the shared settings plus this lab's names:

git clone https://github.com/stefpin/azure-fundamentals-lunches.git   # first time only
cd azure-fundamentals-lunches/labs/18-governance-compliance-basic
source ../common/config.sh
source lab-vars.sh        # RG, RG_ID, DENIED_LOCATION, resource and assignment names
echo "Lab RG: $RG | allowed region: $LOCATION | region used for the denial test: $DENIED_LOCATION"

- Create the starting point — the resource group and two untagged "legacy" resources (about 2 minutes):

bash setup.sh

Important: Lab resources cost money while they exist (here: almost nothing — an empty storage account or two and some network security groups). Finish with the Clean up section, even if you stop halfway. Every assignment in this lab is scoped to the lab resource group, so the rest of your subscription is not affected.

Tip: Cloud Shell forgets your variables when it times out. If a command complains about an empty value, go back to the lab folder and run source ../common/config.sh && source lab-vars.sh again. Task 1 also tells you how to restore the three policy IDs.

Choose your mode

Mode | For you if… | How
Guided | you want every step explained | follow Tasks 1–8 below
Challenge | you already know the basics | read only the Challenge brief, build it your way, then run bash verify.sh

Task 1 · Find the three built-in definitions by display name

Built-in definitions are written and maintained by Microsoft, and they are identified by a GUID. Scripts that copy GUIDs around are hard to read and easy to break, so this course always looks them up by display name. Each az policy definition list call searches thousands of definitions, so give it 10–30 seconds.

First, look at the three definitions — their mode, their parameters and their effect:

az policy definition list \
  --query "[?policyType=='BuiltIn' && contains(['Allowed locations', 'Require a tag on resources', 'Inherit a tag from the resource group if missing'], displayName)].{name:displayName, mode:mode, parameters:join(', ', keys(parameters)), effect:policyRule.then.effect}" \
  --output table

All three use Indexed mode (they look at resources that support tags and locations, not at resource groups). The parameter names — listOfAllowedLocations and tagName — are exactly what you will pass in Tasks 2–4. If Allowed locations shows [parameters('effect')] as its effect, the effect is itself a parameter whose default is Deny; the other two have their effect (deny, modify) written into the rule.

Now store the three IDs. lookup_builtin_ids (defined in lab-vars.sh) runs one query like the one below and sets three variables:

# What lookup_builtin_ids does, for one definition:
az policy definition list --query "[?policyType=='BuiltIn' && displayName=='Allowed locations'].id | [0]" --output tsv

lookup_builtin_ids
printf '%s\n' "$ALLOWED_LOCATIONS_ID" "$REQUIRE_TAG_ID" "$INHERIT_TAG_ID"

Finally, find out which role the Modify policy needs to do its job. The definition lists it in roleDefinitionIds:

ROLE_ID=$(az policy definition list \
  --query "[?id=='$INHERIT_TAG_ID'] | [0].policyRule.then.details.roleDefinitionIds[0]" --output tsv)
az role definition list --query "[?name=='${ROLE_ID##*/}'].roleName | [0]" --output tsv

Tip: Prefer the portal? Policy › Definitions, search for each display name and open it to read the JSON: the if condition, the then effect, the parameters and (for the inherit policy) roleDefinitionIds. Then come back and run lookup_builtin_ids.

Checkpoint: three IDs that start with /providers/Microsoft.Authorization/policyDefinitions/, and the role name Contributor.

Task 2 · Assign "Allowed locations" to the resource group

An assignment connects a definition to a scope and supplies the parameter values. The scope here is the lab resource group, written as a resource ID. Region names must be the programmatic ones (southeastasia, not "Southeast Asia"). The non-compliance message appears inside the error, so people learn what to do instead of filing a ticket.

az policy assignment create \
  --name "$A_LOCATIONS" \
  --display-name "Lunch 18 - Allowed locations" \
  --scope "$RG_ID" \
  --policy "$ALLOWED_LOCATIONS_ID" \
  --params "{ 'listOfAllowedLocations': { 'value': [ '$LOCATION' ] } }" \
  --output none

az policy assignment non-compliance-message create \
  --name "$A_LOCATIONS" \
  --scope "$RG_ID" \
  --message "Nusantara Retail keeps lab resources in $LOCATION. Please choose that region." \
  --output none

Checkpoint: the assignment shows your region and the enforcement mode Default: az policy assignment show --name "$A_LOCATIONS" --scope "$RG_ID" --query "{scope:scope, locations:parameters.listOfAllowedLocations.value, enforcement:enforcementMode}" --output jsonc

Task 3 · Assign "Require a tag on resources"

This one refuses any new or updated resource in the group that has no costCenter tag. It does not apply to the resource group itself.

az policy assignment create \
  --name "$A_REQUIRE_TAG" \
  --display-name "Lunch 18 - Require costCenter tag" \
  --scope "$RG_ID" \
  --policy "$REQUIRE_TAG_ID" \
  --params "{ 'tagName': { 'value': 'costCenter' } }" \
  --output none

Checkpoint: two assignments on the group: az policy assignment list --resource-group "$RG" --query "[].{name:name, displayName:displayName, enforcement:enforcementMode}" --output table

Task 4 · Assign "Inherit a tag from the resource group if missing" with a managed identity

Modify policies change resources for you. Changing a request on the fly needs nothing special, but fixing resources that already exist (Task 7) is done by a remediation task, and that task acts as a managed identity that belongs to the assignment. Three extra flags handle it: --mi-system-assigned creates the identity, --location says where it lives, and --identity-scope plus --role grant it the Contributor role you found in Task 1 — on this resource group only.

az policy assignment create \
  --name "$A_INHERIT_TAG" \
  --display-name "Lunch 18 - Inherit costCenter from the resource group" \
  --scope "$RG_ID" \
  --policy "$INHERIT_TAG_ID" \
  --params "{ 'tagName': { 'value': 'costCenter' } }" \
  --mi-system-assigned \
  --location "$LOCATION" \
  --identity-scope "$RG_ID" \
  --role Contributor \
  --output none

PRINCIPAL_ID=$(az policy assignment show --name "$A_INHERIT_TAG" --scope "$RG_ID" --query identity.principalId --output tsv)
az role assignment list --scope "$RG_ID" \
  --query "[?principalId=='$PRINCIPAL_ID'].{role:roleDefinitionName, scope:scope}" --output table

Tip: Prefer the portal? Policy › Assignments › Assign policy. On the Remediation tab, keep System assigned managed identity, pick your region, and the portal grants the roles from roleDefinitionIds automatically.

Checkpoint: one row with role Contributor at your resource group's scope. If the list is empty, the new identity was probably still replicating in Microsoft Entra ID: wait a minute and run az role assignment create --assignee-object-id "$PRINCIPAL_ID" --assignee-principal-type ServicePrincipal --role Contributor --scope "$RG_ID".

Task 5 · Wait for the guardrails, then prove the denials

A new assignment takes about five minutes — sometimes longer — to reach its scope. Instead of guessing, ask Azure Resource Manager to validate (not deploy) a tiny template with a network security group in the forbidden region. Validation runs the same Deny checks as a real deployment and creates nothing. This loop checks every 30 seconds:

for i in $(seq 1 30); do
  out=$(az deployment group validate --resource-group "$RG" --template-file policy-probe.json \
        --parameters location="$DENIED_LOCATION" --only-show-errors --output none 2>&1)
  if grep -qiE "RequestDisallowedByPolicy|disallowed by policy|policy violation" <<<"$out"; then
    echo "Allowed locations is enforced now."; break
  elif [ -n "$out" ]; then
    echo "$out"; break
  fi
  echo "Not enforced yet (check $i of 30) - trying again in 30 seconds..."; sleep 30
done

While you wait, re-read Effects in the lunch: which of your three assignments will act before the request reaches the storage resource provider?

5a · The wrong region. Ask for a storage account in the forbidden region. It even carries the right tag, so only the location rule can object:

az storage account create --name "$DENIED_SA" --resource-group "$RG" \
  --location "$DENIED_LOCATION" --sku Standard_LRS --tags costCenter="$COST_CENTER"

You should get an error that starts with (RequestDisallowedByPolicy) Resource 'stdenied…' was disallowed by policy. Read on: it names the assignment Lunch 18 - Allowed locations and shows your non-compliance message. Your Owner role did not help — RBAC said yes, the policy said no.

5b · The missing tag. Ask for a network security group in the right region, without tags:

az network nsg create --name nsg-untagged --resource-group "$RG" --location "$LOCATION"

This time the error names Lunch 18 - Require costCenter tag. The inherit policy could not help, because the resource group itself has no costCenter tag yet — there was nothing to copy.

Checkpoint: two RequestDisallowedByPolicy errors, and nothing new in the group: az resource list --resource-group "$RG" --query "[].name" --output tsv still shows only the two legacy resources. If 5b succeeded instead, the tag rule was not enforced yet: delete it with az network nsg delete --name nsg-untagged --resource-group "$RG", wait two minutes and try again.

Task 6 · Create compliant resources — and let Modify do the work

First the obvious way: right region, right tag.

az storage account create --name "$COMPLIANT_SA" --resource-group "$RG" --location "$LOCATION" \
  --sku Standard_LRS --kind StorageV2 --min-tls-version TLS1_2 --allow-blob-public-access false \
  --tags costCenter="$COST_CENTER" --output none

Now the convenient way. Tag the resource group once (Merge keeps its existing tags), then run the command that failed in 5b again, under a new name and still without tags:

az tag update --resource-id "$RG_ID" --operation Merge --tags costCenter="$COST_CENTER" --output none
az group show --name "$RG" --query tags --output jsonc

az network nsg create --name nsg-app --resource-group "$RG" --location "$LOCATION" --output none
az network nsg show --name nsg-app --resource-group "$RG" --query tags --output jsonc

Azure Policy runs Modify before Deny: the inherit policy copied costCenter from the resource group into the request, so the require policy found the tag and let it through.

Checkpoint: nsg-app shows "costCenter": "CC-1001" although you never typed it. If nsg-app is still refused straight after you tagged the group, wait a minute and run the create command again.

Task 7 · Remediate the legacy resources

stlegacy… and nsg-legacy existed before the rules, so no request ever passed through the Modify policy for them. Deny and Modify never touch existing resources on their own; they only report them. Look at the report first:

az policy state list --resource-group "$RG" --filter "complianceState eq 'NonCompliant'" \
  --query "[].{assignment:policyAssignmentName, type:resourceType}" --output table

You should see the legacy resources listed for the tag assignments (if the list is empty, the first evaluation is still running — continue anyway). A remediation task fixes them in bulk through the assignment's managed identity. ReEvaluateCompliance makes it re-check every resource first, so you do not have to wait for a scan:

INHERIT_ASSIGNMENT_ID=$(az policy assignment show --name "$A_INHERIT_TAG" --scope "$RG_ID" --query id --output tsv)

az policy remediation create \
  --name "$REMEDIATION" \
  --resource-group "$RG" \
  --policy-assignment "$INHERIT_ASSIGNMENT_ID" \
  --resource-discovery-mode ReEvaluateCompliance \
  --output none

Check the task every minute or so. It usually finishes within 2–10 minutes:

az policy remediation show --name "$REMEDIATION" --resource-group "$RG" \
  --query "{state:provisioningState, deployments:deploymentStatus}" --output jsonc

When the state is Succeeded, look at the tags:

az resource list --resource-group "$RG" \
  --query "[].{name:name, location:location, costCenter:tags.costCenter}" --output table

Tip: Prefer the portal? Policy › Remediation lists every Modify and DeployIfNotExists assignment with resources to fix. The Remediation tasks tab shows progress and links to each change.

Checkpoint: every resource in the table — including stlegacy… and nsg-legacy — shows CC-1001, and the remediation task shows Succeeded.

Task 8 · Read the compliance results

Compliance results refresh after changes, after new assignments, once a day and on demand. Ask for an on-demand scan of your resource group; the command waits until the scan is done, which usually takes a few minutes:

az policy state trigger-scan --resource-group "$RG"

az policy state summarize --resource-group "$RG" --query "results || value[0].results" --output jsonc

az policy state list --resource-group "$RG" \
  --query "[].{assignment:policyAssignmentName, state:complianceState, type:resourceType}" --output table

summarize gives the auditor's view: how many resources and policies are non-compliant (resourceDetails counts them per state). list gives the engineer's view: one record per resource and assignment.

Tip: Prefer the portal? Policy › Compliance, set the scope to your resource group, and open each assignment. The Resource compliance tab shows every resource and its state; Compliance details explains why.

Checkpoint: compliance records exist for all three assignments, and every resource is Compliant. A non-compliant record usually means a scan or the remediation task is still catching up — run the scan again in a few minutes.

Break it and fix it

Someone "tidies up" the resource group and deletes its costCenter tag. The next day Dewi's pipeline — the same one that worked in Task 6 — fails. Reproduce it:

az tag update --resource-id "$RG_ID" --operation Delete --tags costCenter="$COST_CENTER" --output none
az network nsg create --name nsg-breakfix --resource-group "$RG" --location "$LOCATION" --output none

Symptom: RequestDisallowedByPolicy, naming Lunch 18 - Require costCenter tag. The existing resources are fine — they keep their tags.

Hint

The inherit policy copies the tag from the resource group. With no tag on the group there is nothing to copy, so the request reaches the Deny rule unchanged. Fix the source, not the pipeline: put the tag back on the group, wait a minute, and run the nsg create command again. It succeeds, and nsg-breakfix gets costCenter automatically.

az tag update --resource-id "$RG_ID" --operation Merge --tags costCenter="$COST_CENTER" --output none

In production, protect the source too — for example with the built-in Require a tag on resource groups policy at subscription scope.

Verify your work

bash verify.sh

Every check should say PASS. If one fails, the message tells you which task to revisit. The compliance checks need evaluation results — if they fail, run az policy state trigger-scan --resource-group "$RG" and try again a few minutes later.

Clean up (do not skip!)

bash cleanup.sh

This removes the role assignment of the inherit policy's managed identity, the three policy assignments and the resource group rg-lunch18-<suffix> with everything in it (including remediation tasks and any lock you added in the stretch goals). Deletion continues in the background for a few minutes.

Troubleshooting

Symptom | Likely cause | Fix
(RequestDisallowedByPolicy) Resource 'stnusa…' was disallowed by policy in Task 6 | the command lacks --tags costCenter=…, or uses another region | add the tag and use --location "$LOCATION"
The storage account in $DENIED_LOCATION was created in Task 5a | the assignment was not enforced yet | delete it: az storage account delete --name "$DENIED_SA" --resource-group "$RG" --yes, run the probe loop, try again
AuthorizationFailed … Microsoft.Authorization/roleAssignments/write in Task 4 | you are not Owner or User Access Administrator, so the CLI cannot grant the identity its role | use a subscription you own, or ask an Owner to grant Contributor on the resource group to the identity
PrincipalNotFound in Task 4 | the brand-new managed identity has not replicated in Microsoft Entra ID yet | wait a minute, then run the az role assignment create command from the Task 4 checkpoint
InvalidCreatePolicyAssignmentRequest mentioning a managed identity | the Modify assignment was created without --mi-system-assigned and --location | run the Task 4 command exactly as shown
The subscription is not registered to use namespace 'Microsoft.PolicyInsights' | the resource provider is not registered yet | az provider register --namespace Microsoft.PolicyInsights, wait a minute or two (setup.sh does this)
Remediation state Failed; deploymentStatus shows failed deployments | the identity has no role on the resource group | fix the Task 4 checkpoint, then create a new remediation task with a different --name
az policy state list returns [] | no evaluation has finished yet | az policy state trigger-scan --resource-group "$RG", then wait
(StorageAccountAlreadyTaken) | someone else uses that global name | pick another name, for example COMPLIANT_SA="stnusa${SUFFIX}x"
The probe loop prints an error and stops | usually the wrong folder (policy-probe.json not found) | cd into labs/18-governance-compliance-basic and run it again

Stretch goals

- Report before you enforce. Switch Allowed locations to report-only, wait about five minutes, create a storage account in $DENIED_LOCATION (it now succeeds), scan, and find it as non-compliant. Then switch back and delete it: az policy assignment update --name "$A_LOCATIONS" --scope "$RG_ID" --enforcement-mode DoNotEnforce (and later --enforcement-mode Default).
- Exempt one resource. Give stnusa… a Waiver exemption from the tag rule that expires tomorrow, and watch it turn Exempt after a scan: az policy exemption create --name tag-waiver --policy-assignment "$(az policy assignment show --name "$A_REQUIRE_TAG" --scope "$RG_ID" --query id --output tsv)" --exemption-category Waiver --scope "$(az storage account show --name "$COMPLIANT_SA" --resource-group "$RG" --query id --output tsv)" --expires-on "$(date -u -d '+1 day' +%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ)".
- Lock it. Add az lock create --name no-delete --lock-type CanNotDelete --resource-group "$RG", then try to delete nsg-app and read the ScopeLocked error. cleanup.sh removes the lock for you.
- Explore regulatory initiatives: az policy set-definition list --query "[?policyType=='BuiltIn' && metadata.category=='Regulatory Compliance'].displayName" --output tsv | sort | head -n 20.

Challenge brief

Build the following, any way you like (portal, CLI, Bicep). Start with bash setup.sh.

1. On rg-lunch18-<suffix>, assign the built-in Allowed locations policy so that resources can only be created in your lab region ($LOCATION).
2. On the same resource group, assign Require a tag on resources for the tag costCenter.
3. On the same resource group, assign Inherit a tag from the resource group if missing for costCenter, with a system-assigned managed identity that holds the role the definition asks for on the resource group.
4. Show that a storage account in another region is refused, then create a compliant storage account (not the legacy one) in $LOCATION.
5. Tag the resource group costCenter=CC-1001 and use a remediation task so that both legacy resources from setup.sh carry the tag.
6. Make sure compliance results exist for all three assignments.

Then run bash verify.sh. Stuck? Peek at solution.sh or switch to Guided mode.
